- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text:
I have completed a thorough search. Here are my findings.

## Summary

This is the **memos** project (Go backend using the Connect/gRPC framework + Echo v5 for HTTP; React frontend in `web/`). There is **no true API rate-limiting / throttling middleware anywhere** — no per-user, per-IP, per-endpoint, global, or login-attempt rate limiting exists. No rate-limiting library is imported (no `express-rate-limit`, `tollbooth`, `ulule/limiter`, `golang.org/x/time/rate`, etc. — confirmed absent from `go.mod`/`go.sum`).

### 1. Per-user API rate-limiting middleware: NONE

The complete server middleware/interceptor chain contains no rate limiter:

- **Echo HTTP middleware** — `/bench/repo/server/server.go:51-52`: only `middleware.Recover()` and `newCORSMiddleware(profile)`. Nothing else.
- **Connect RPC interceptor chain** — `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:133-137`:
  ```
  connect.WithInterceptors(
      NewMetadataInterceptor(),   // header -> gRPC metadata
      NewLoggingInterceptor(...),
      NewRecoveryInterceptor(...),
      NewAuthInterceptor(authorizer),
  )
  ```
  These four interceptors (defined in `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/connect_interceptors.go`) do metadata conversion, logging, panic recovery, and authentication only. No rate/throttle interceptor.

### 2. What limiting DOES exist (concurrency limits, not rate limits)

The only throttling-like logic is **global in-process concurrency semaphores** on image work, meant to prevent memory exhaustion — not request-rate limits, and not scoped per user or per IP.

- **Definitions** — `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:39-41` and `59-60`:
  - `thumbnailSemaphore = semaphore.NewWeighted(3)` — "Limit to 3 concurrent thumbnail generations". **Note: this semaphore is declared but never actually acquired anywhere** (no `.Acquire` call exists in the codebase — it is effectively dead/unused).
  - `imageProcessingSemaphore = semaphore.NewWeighted(2)` — limits concurrent EXIF-stripping/image processing to **2 concurrent operations**.
- **Enforcement of the image-processing limit** — `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/attachment_service_image.go:67-77` (`acquireImageProcessingSlot`, which does `imageProcessingSemaphore.Acquire(ctx, 1)`), invoked from `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/attachment_service.go:158-160`. On failure it returns `codes.ResourceExhausted, "too many image processing requests"`.

  Scope: this is a **single process-wide (global) limit of 2 simultaneous image-processing operations across ALL users/requests combined** — it is not per-user, not per-IP, and not a rate (requests/time) limit. It only bounds concurrency, and only when EXIF stripping runs on image uploads.

### 3. Login / auth: NO limiting

`/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/auth_service.go` and `/bench/repo/server/auth/*.go` contain **no** failed-login throttling, lockout, backoff, or attempt counting. The word "attempt" appears only in a doc comment (`/bench/repo/server/auth/authenticator.go:126`).

### 4. Email: aspirational only, not implemented

`/bench/repo/internal/email/doc.go:86` lists "Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse" as a security *recommendation* in a doc comment. There is **no actual email rate-limiting code** in `internal/email/` or `server/notification/`.

### Other notes
- Frontend hits for "limit" (`web/src/components/MemoEditor/Editor/listIndent.ts`, `formatting.ts`) are unrelated (text-editor indent/formatting limits).
- No `429`/`StatusTooManyRequests` HTTP handling exists; the only `ResourceExhausted` usages are the image-processing semaphore (`attachment_service.go:160`) and the interceptor's error-code mapping table (`connect_interceptors.go:153`).
- No deployment-level rate limiting (no nginx `limit_req`/`limit_conn`, no Caddy throttle) found in any config/Dockerfile.

**Bottom line:** No per-user (or any) API request rate limiting exists. The only "limit" is a global concurrency cap of 2 simultaneous image-processing operations (`v1.go:60`, enforced at `attachment_service.go:158-160`), plus an unused thumbnail concurrency semaphore of 3 (`v1.go:59`).

**Premise correction:** The question assumes this repository has per-user API rate-limiting middleware. It does not. No API rate limiting of any kind — per-user, per-IP, per-endpoint, global, or login-attempt — exists anywhere in the codebase, and no rate-limiting library is imported (confirmed absent from `go.mod`/`go.sum`).

This is the **memos** project: a Go backend (Connect/gRPC + Echo v5) with a React frontend. The complete server middleware/interceptor chain contains no limiter:

- **Echo HTTP middleware** (`server/server.go:51-52`): only `middleware.Recover()` and `newCORSMiddleware(profile)`.
- **Connect RPC interceptors** (`server/router/api/v1/v1.go:133-137`): `NewMetadataInterceptor`, `NewLoggingInterceptor`, `NewRecoveryInterceptor`, `NewAuthInterceptor` — metadata conversion, logging, panic recovery, and authentication only. Defined in `server/router/api/v1/connect_interceptors.go`.
- **Auth/login** (`server/router/api/v1/auth_service.go`, `server/auth/*.go`): no failed-login throttling, lockout, or attempt counting.

**The only "limits" that exist are in-process concurrency semaphores, not request-rate limits:**

- `imageProcessingSemaphore = semaphore.NewWeighted(2)` (`server/router/api/v1/v1.go:59-60`) — caps **image processing (EXIF stripping) at 2 concurrent operations process-wide**, across all users combined. Acquired in `attachment_service_image.go:67-77` and invoked from `attachment_service.go:158-160`; on exhaustion it returns `codes.ResourceExhausted, "too many image processing requests"`.
- `thumbnailSemaphore = semaphore.NewWeighted(3)` (`v1.go:39-41`) — declared for 3 concurrent thumbnail generations but **never actually acquired anywhere** (effectively dead code).

These are global concurrency caps meant to prevent memory exhaustion — they are not per-user, not per-IP, and not rate (requests-per-time) limits. There is also no `429`/`StatusTooManyRequests` handling and no deployment-level throttling (no nginx `limit_req`, no Caddy config) in the repo.

So: there is no per-user rate-limiting middleware to point to. The closest thing is a global cap of 2 concurrent image-processing operations.
